title: ELSS Outflows: Are Tax-Saving Mutual Funds Losing Relevance?
description: Equity Linked Savings Schemes (ELSS) have seen significant net outflows recently, with ₹650 crore redeemed in May alone. This trend suggests a potential shift.

faq.q: What is the lock-in period for ELSS funds?
faq.a: ELSS funds have a mandatory lock-in period of three years from the date of investment. This is the shortest lock-in among all Section 80C tax-saving instruments.

faq.q: Is ELSS still relevant under the New Tax Regime?
faq.a: No, if you choose the New Tax Regime, you cannot claim deductions under Section 80C, so ELSS loses its primary tax-saving advantage. However, it still functions as an equity mutual fund for wealth creation.
Long-term capital gains (LTCG) from ELSS, exceeding ₹1 lakh in a financial year, are taxed at 10% without indexation. Dividends, if any, are taxed as per the investor's income slab.

faq.q: Can I invest in ELSS through SIP?
faq.a: Yes, you can invest in ELSS through a Systematic Investment Plan (SIP). Each SIP instalment will have its own three-year lock-in period from its respective investment date.

faq.q: What happens if I redeem ELSS before the lock-in?
faq.a: You cannot redeem ELSS units before the completion of the three-year lock-in period. Premature withdrawal is not permitted under any circumstances.

faq.q: Should I switch from ELSS to another fund after lock-in?
faq.a: This depends on your financial goals, risk appetite, and market outlook. If you need the funds or prefer a different investment strategy, you can redeem and reinvest. If your goals align with continued equity exposure, you can remain invested.

faq.q: Are ELSS funds suitable for conservative investors?
faq.a: ELSS funds invest primarily in equities, making them subject to market risks. They are generally more suitable for investors with a moderate to high-risk appetite and a long-term investment horizon.
